content: 1. Atropine and Aclidinium: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Close monitoring is advised due to the potential for additive anticholinergic effects. 2. Atropine and Amantadine: These drugs exhibit pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of anticholinergic adverse effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Atropine and Amitriptyline: Both decrease cholinergic transmission. Amitriptyline may also increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely for potential additive effects. 4. Atropine and Amoxapine: Both reduce cholinergic effects, and amoxapine may increase atropine levels by an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 5. Atropine and Anticholinergic/Sedative Combinations: These combinations can lead to additive anticholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Atropine and Aripiprazole: Atropine decreases aripiprazole levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Aripiprazole may increase atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely, especially for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 7. Atropine and Atenolol: Atropine may increase atenolol levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 8. Atropine and Atracurium: Both drugs reduce cholinergic transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Atropine and Belladonna Alkaloids: These drugs decrease cholinergic effects. Monitor closely and use caution. 10. Atropine and Benperidol: Atropine reduces benperidol levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Benperidol increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 11. Atropine and Benzotropine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects, potentially leading to additive anticholinergic adverse effects. Monitor closely. 12. Atropine and Bethanechol: Bethanechol increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 13. Atropine and Buprenorphine (Long-Acting Injection): Buprenorphine increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Co-administration may increase the risk of urinary retention and/or severe constipation, potentially leading to paralytic ileus. Monitor closely. 14. Atropine and Carbachol: Carbachol increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 15. Atropine and Cevimeline: Cevimeline increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 16. Atropine and Chlorpromazine: Atropine reduces chlorpromazine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Chlorpromazine increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 17. Atropine and Cisatracurium: Both drugs reduce cholinergic transmission. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Atropine and Clomipramine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Clomipramine may increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 19. Atropine and Clozapine: Atropine reduces clozapine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Clozapine increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 20. Atropine and Cyclizine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Atropine and Cyclobenzaprine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 22. Atropine and Darifenacin: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Atropine and DaxibotulinumtoxinA: Atropine increases the effects of daxibotulinumtoxinA via pharmacodynamic synergy. Drugs with anticholinergic effects may potentiate botulinum toxin effects, leading to excessive neuromuscular weakness and heightened systemic anticholinergic effects. Monitor closely. 24. Atropine and Desipramine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Desipramine may increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 25. Atropine and Dicyclomine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 26. Atropine and Digoxin: Atropine may increase digoxin levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 27. Atropine and Dimenhydrinate: Dimenhydrinate may increase atropine toxicity via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects. 28. Atropine and Diphenhydramine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 29. Atropine and Donepezil: Donepezil increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 30. Atropine and Dosulepin: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Atropine and Doxepin: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Doxepin may increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 32. Atropine and Droperidol: Atropine reduces droperidol levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Droperidol increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 33. Atropine and Echothiophate Iodide: Echothiophate increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 34. Atropine and Eluxadoline: Both drugs may increase each other's effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Co-administration increases the risk of constipation-related serious adverse reactions. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 35. Atropine and Fentanyl: Co-administration may increase the risk of urinary retention and/or severe constipation, potentially leading to paralytic ileus. Monitor closely. 36. Atropine and Fesoterodine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 37. Atropine and Fluphenazine: Atropine reduces fluphenazine levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Fluphenazine increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 38. Atropine and Galantamine: Galantamine increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 39. Atropine and Glucagon: Co-administration with anticholinergic drugs increases the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions due to additive effects on gastrointestinal motility inhibition. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 40. Atropine and Glycopyrrolate: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 41. Atropine and Haloperidol: Atropine reduces haloperidol levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Haloperidol increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 42. Atropine and Huperzine A: Huperzine A increases cholinergic effects, while atropine decreases them. The interaction effect is unclear, so use caution and monitor closely. 45. Atropine and Hyoscyamine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 46. Atropine and Iloperidone: Atropine reduces iloperidone levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Iloperidone increases atropine effects via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for additive anticholinergic effects and possible hypoglycemia. 47. Atropine and Imipramine: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Imipramine may increase atropine levels through an unknown mechanism. Monitor closely. 48. Atropine and IncobotulinumtoxinA: Atropine increases the effects of incobotulinumtoxinA via pharmacodynamic synergy. Monitor closely for excessive neuromuscular weakness and systemic anticholinergic effects. 49. Atropine and Ipratropium: Both drugs reduce cholinergic effects. Due to poor systemic absorption of ipratropium, interaction is unlikely at recommended dosages. Monitor closely. 50. Atropine and Levodopa: Anticholinergic agents may enhance the therapeutic effects of levodopa but can exacerbate tardive dyskinesia. At high doses, anticholinergics may decrease levodopa effects by delaying gastrointestinal absorption. Monitor closely. This list continues with similar interactions, emphasizing the need for caution, close monitoring, and in some cases, avoiding co-administration due to additive anticholinergic effects or other pharmacodynamic interactions.
